title: Abstraction and Encapsulation
learningObjectives: Explain abstraction as exposing essential behavior while hiding unnecessary detail.
Describe encapsulation as protecting internal state and enforcing rules.
Recognize when internal details should not be exposed.
Apply abstraction and encapsulation to a small example.

understand.concept: Abstraction focuses attention on what a component offers rather than every implementation detail. Encapsulation groups state and behavior and controls how internal state is accessed or changed. A public interface provides supported operations; callers do not need to know how those operations are implemented. Encapsulation is not merely making properties private: it also helps enforce invariants and prevent invalid state. Use language-supported mechanisms appropriate to the project.
understand.whyItMatters: Focused responsibilities and controlled boundaries make software easier to change, test, and explain.
understand.analogy: A well-organized workshop keeps tools and tasks arranged so each job can be completed without disturbing unrelated work.
understand.analogyLimit: Real software components exchange data and have technical constraints that a physical workshop analogy cannot fully capture.

explain.narrative: A caller can use a deposit method without knowing how a balance is stored. The method is an abstraction; controlled access to the balance is encapsulation. A well-designed interface keeps essential behavior visible while protecting details that callers should not modify directly. Avoid hiding everything: the interface should remain understandable and useful.

examples.title: Simple abstraction
examples.explanation: The caller uses a meaningful operation without seeing extra details.

examples.title: Encapsulate state with closure
examples.explanation: The count is not directly exposed; the returned function controls changes.

examples.title: Expose a supported operation
examples.code:
class Wallet{#balance=0; add(amount){if(amount>0)this.#balance+=amount;} getBalance(){return this.#balance;}}
const w=new Wallet();w.add(5);console.log(w.getBalance());
examples.explanation: Methods provide controlled access to private state.

examples.title: Protect an invariant
examples.code:
class Box{#items=[]; add(item){if(item!=null)this.#items.push(item;} size(){return this.#items.length;}}
const b=new Box();b.add('x');console.log(b.size());
examples.explanation: The class controls how its internal collection is modified.

examples.title: Hide implementation behind a function
examples.explanation: Callers depend on the operation's result, not the formula details.

commonMistakes: Making boundaries too small or too large without a reason.
Allowing components to rely on hidden state.
Mixing unrelated responsibilities in one function.
Exposing internal data that callers can modify unexpectedly.
Treating a design guideline as a rigid rule instead of a contextual trade-off.

guidedTask.instructions: Choose a state value callers should not modify directly. Write a small interface with one or two operations. independentTask.instructions: Create a small account, counter, or task-list abstraction. Keep internal state private or controlled. Provide methods that enforce valid changes. Demonstrate normal and rejected input behavior. Describe the public interface without exposing implementation internals.
